summary: An experimental protocol, the Script MIB Extensibility Protocol (SMX), that separates language-specific runtime systems from language-independent Script MIB implementations. It was replaced by RFC 3179.

eli5.summary: This is a go-between that lets the script system work with different programming languages without being rebuilt for each one.

questions: how does smx separate languages from management systems
how do snmp agents run scripts
subtitle: A protocol that lets management scripts work with multiple programming languages without rebuilding

tldr.problem: The Script MIB allows SNMP agents to run management scripts, but the MIB itself was language-agnostic; implementations would need rewriting to support Tcl, Java, Perl, or other languages.
tldr.mechanism: SMX (Script MIB Extensibility Protocol) separates the language-independent SNMP agent code from language-specific runtime systems. The agent and each runtime system (Java VM, Tcl interpreter) communicate over a simple text protocol, allowing new languages to be plugged in without changing the agent.
tldr.outcome: This experimental protocol was replaced by RFC 3179 but established a pattern for language-independent protocol extensibility that influenced later work.

today: RFC 2593 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 3179. The concept of separating protocol implementations from language runtimes via simple text protocols influenced later extensibility standards and continues in tools like remote procedure call frameworks.

sections.title: The Script MIB and the Language Problem
sections.content:
RFC 2592 defines the Script MIB, which lets network administrators send management scripts to SNMP agents and have them executed remotely. The MIB defines the data structures and operations for script transfer, execution, monitoring, and termination—but says nothing about which programming language the scripts use.

The practical problem: when an SNMP agent needed to run scripts written in Java, Tcl, Python, or other languages, the agent implementation itself had to be rebuilt for each language or had to bundle multiple runtime systems. SMX solves this by defining a lightweight protocol that lets the agent (written in one language) communicate with separate runtime system processes (Java VM, Tcl interpreter, etc.) without knowing which language they use.
sections.eli5: Network managers want to send scripts to routers and switches and have them run. The scripts could be written in different languages (Java, Tcl, etc.). SMX is a simple bridge that lets the router run scripts in any language by talking to a language interpreter in a standard way.

sections.title: Process and Communication Architecture
sections.content:
The SMX architecture separates three components: (1) the SNMP agent with the Script MIB, (2) one or more runtime systems (Java VM, Tcl interpreter, etc.), and (3) a shared local script storage device (usually a file system directory).

When the agent wants to run a script, it writes the script to local storage, then sends an SMX message over a TCP connection telling a runtime system where to find it and how to run it. The runtime system reads the script, executes it, and sends back status messages and results. Scripts can be suspended, resumed, or aborted through SMX commands. Each runtime system can run multiple scripts concurrently if it supports multi-threading.
sections.eli5: The SNMP agent puts a script on the hard disk, then tells the Java interpreter (or Tcl interpreter) to run it. The interpreter runs the script and tells the agent what happened. Everything is local, so it is secure.

sections.title: Security Profiles and Operation
sections.content:
SMX supports two layers of security control. Operating system security profiles determine what file system and system resources a script can access (mapped to Unix user/group identity and resource limits). Runtime system security profiles (Java SecurityManager, safe Tcl interpreter) provide fine-grained control over what the script can do while running.

Connection establishment is protected: the agent creates a listening TCP socket on localhost (only local connections allowed), generates a random security cookie, and passes it to the runtime system via environment variables. The runtime system must return the correct cookie; if not, the connection is rejected. This prevents unauthorized runtime systems from connecting.
sections.eli5: Two layers of protection: the operating system decides what files a script can use, and the language interpreter decides what the script can do. Plus, only runtime systems that know a secret cookie can connect, so no random process can inject scripts.

sections.title: SMX Protocol Messages and Commands
sections.content:
SMX uses a simple text-based protocol with commands sent from the agent to runtime systems and replies sent back. The first command is always hello, which identifies the runtime system and exchanges authentication. Then the agent can send start (run a script), suspend, resume, abort, and status commands.

Replies use three-digit codes similar to SMTP: 2yz for success, 4yz for permanent errors, 5yz for asynchronous notifications. For example, a 231 reply reports script status changes, while a 534 reply announces normal script termination with results. The protocol supports both human-readable quoted strings and hex-encoded binary data for arguments and results, allowing scripts to pass any kind of data back to the agent.
sections.eli5: SMX is a simple chat protocol. The agent says "hello" and the interpreter says who it is. Then the agent says "run this script here" and the interpreter says "done" or "error". Everything is text and numbers.

sections.title: Message Flow and Practical Use
sections.content:
A typical SMX conversation begins with hello and a cookie exchange. The agent then sends start commands with script file paths and security profiles. Multiple scripts can be launched in parallel. The runtime system sends 231 replies to report state changes, 532 for intermediate results, and 534 for normal termination or 535 for abnormal termination with error codes.

The agent can suspend and resume scripts, or abort them if a timeout occurs. All commands include a transaction ID so the agent can correlate replies with requests. The protocol is designed to be simple enough that any language's runtime can implement it, whether single-threaded or multi-threaded, and it runs entirely on localhost so encryption is not mandatory (though TLS could wrap it if needed).
sections.eli5: A script runs, sends back status messages, and finishes. The agent can pause it, wake it up, or kill it. Everything happens on the local machine so there is no risk of messages being intercepted on the network.
